title: A systematic review of AI-assisted academic writing: Tools, measures, and effects
finding: Across 25 included empirical studies, effects were more consistently positive for psychological and writing-process outcomes than for textual products. Product gains were clearest for surface accuracy and conventions, while higher-order argumentation and discourse-organization results were mixed.
implication: Humanvoice must separate process, surface, and higher-order outcomes and validate on research manuscripts rather than importing results from course essays.

title: Generative artificial intelligence for automated writing evaluation: A systematic review of trends, efficacy, and challenges
finding: The review reports stronger performance for grammar, coherence, and rubric-based tasks than for higher-order argumentation and creativity, with unresolved validity, fairness, equity, and integrity concerns for consequential assessment.
implication: Automated feedback can triage surface issues, but Humanvoice must calibrate higher-order judgments against domain readers and prohibit model-only release decisions.

title: Prototypical Human-AI Collaboration Behaviors from LLM-Assisted Writing in the Wild
finding: Large-scale in-the-wild writing sessions show recurring multi-turn behaviors in which users revise intents, explore text, ask questions, adjust style, or inject content; a small set of interaction patterns explains much of the observed variation.
implication: The product should retain turn-level intent, suggestion, acceptance, edit, and rejection traces instead of evaluating only the final document.

title: Generative AI at Work
finding: Access to a conversational assistant increased average issues resolved per hour by 15 percent, with larger speed and quality gains for less experienced workers and small quality declines among the highest-skilled workers.
implication: Pilot results must be reported by baseline skill and task slice; an average productivity effect can conceal losses for expert writers.
